title: RJD MP Sanjay Yadav Asks President to Act Against DU Professor Sangeet Ragi
excerpt: In a three-page letter dated November 6, Rajya Sabha member Sanjay Yadav asked President Droupadi Murmu, as Visitor of Delhi University, for an impartial inquiry into allegedly caste-based derogatory remarks by Professor Sangeet Ragi in a televised debate.
body:
• RJD leader and Rajya Sabha member Sanjay Yadav wrote to President Droupadi Murmu on November 6, 2026, seeking strict action against Delhi University Professor Sangeet Ragi for allegedly insulting the Yadav community during a televised debate.
  • The three-page letter, shared with the media on Saturday, November 7, asks the President to intervene as Visitor of the University of Delhi so an impartial inquiry is undertaken.
  • The letter says the remarks reportedly included the expression "gawar" used with the term "Ahir", and accuses Ragi of habitually making derogatory remarks about women, Dalit and Bahujan communities in TV debates.
  • The row has already reached the campus: Ragi's office was ransacked on Wednesday after the debate, and students submitted a memorandum demanding his suspension.

Rashtriya Janata Dal (RJD) leader and Rajya Sabha member Sanjay Yadav has written to President Droupadi Murmu requesting strict action against Delhi University Professor Sangeet Ragi for allegedly insulting the Yadav community during a televised public debate. The three-page letter, dated November 6, was shared with the media on Saturday, November 7, according to The Hindu.

"I request your kind intervention in your capacity as Visitor of the University of Delhi so that an impartial inquiry is undertaken and appropriate action is considered in accordance with the Constitution, applicable laws and university regulations."

— Sanjay Yadav, RJD Rajya Sabha MP, in his letter to the President

What the letter alleges

Yadav, who is also political advisor to Bihar's Leader of Opposition Tejashwi Yadav, wrote that he was expressing "serious concern regarding the alleged caste-based derogatory remarks made by Professor Sangeet Ragi of the University of Delhi against India's largest community (Yadav/Ahir) during a televised public debate." According to media reports cited in the letter, the remarks reportedly included the use of "gawar" in conjunction with "Ahir." Yadav said Ragi used the abusive language against the Yadav community on behalf of the RSS and the BJP, and argued that action is necessary as an exemplary punishment so that no one dares to insult any community in the name of freedom of expression. He also wrote that among academic circles there is a growing demand that Ragi's PhD theses undergo a comprehensive, de novo re-investigation of methodology, facts and sources.

The campus fallout came first

The letter follows days of protest at Delhi University. On Wednesday, Ragi's office was ransacked after a heated argument with Samajwadi Party spokesperson Manoj Kaka during a debate on ABP, and students submitted a memorandum to the Vice-Chancellor demanding his immediate suspension, according to DU Beat. Ragi, a senior professor in the Department of Political Science and its former head, told the Times of India the protesters were angry about his remarks during the debate, which he admitted he should not have made. Activists of the Samajwadi Chhatra Sabha also protested outside Lucknow University, burning his effigy.

What happens next

The route Yadav has chosen is the one the university's structure provides: the President of India is the Visitor of Delhi University, with the authority to cause an inquiry into matters connected with the university. Whether an inquiry is ordered, and what Delhi University itself does about the students' suspension demand, are the decisions to watch. Yadav's letter frames the principle at stake plainly: freedom of expression is an essential democratic right, but universities must be spaces where differences are debated through reason and evidence rather than caste-based ridicule.
nri_angle: For diaspora readers who studied at Delhi University or follow caste and campus politics from abroad, the case tests how India's central universities handle televised conduct by senior faculty.
author: Diaspora Desk
